title: From Doubling Time to R0: Reading the First Weeks of COVID-19 in Wuhan
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Early Transmission Dynamics in Wuhan, China, of Novel Coronavirus–Infected Pneumonia
source.authors: Qun Li, Xuhua Guan, Peng Wu, et al.

intro.summary: In January 2020 a new coronavirus pneumonia was spreading in Wuhan, and nobody yet knew how easily it passed between people. The authors gathered detailed records on the first 425 laboratory-confirmed cases: who they were, what they were exposed to, and when they fell ill. From these records they estimated how long infection takes to cause symptoms, how far apart linked cases fall ill, how fast the epidemic was doubling, and how many people each case infects on average. They found that the epidemic doubled about every 7.4 days and that each case infected about 2.2 others, which is clear evidence of human-to-human spread from mid-December. Several key numbers rest on very few cases (10 for the incubation period, 6 pairs for the serial interval), so the uncertainty ranges are wide, and mild or unusual infections were probably missed.
background: An epidemic grows exponentially when every case passes the infection on to more than one new person, so the count keeps multiplying.
Epidemiologists describe that growth with the doubling time, which is how many days it takes for the number of new cases to double.
The basic reproductive number, R0, is the average number of people one case infects in a population where nobody is yet immune.
Case counts always lag behind real infections, because people need time to fall ill, see a doctor, get tested and be reported.
intro.aha: Just by timing how fast cases doubled and how many days apart linked patients fell ill, you can work out that each case was infecting about two other people, without ever watching a single infection happen.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: In late December 2019, hospitals in Wuhan, a city of 11 million, reported pneumonia cases with no known cause. Most were linked to one seafood market. Health officials urgently needed to know two things. Was the virus only jumping from animals at the market, or was it also passing from person to person? And how fast was it spreading?
primer.quote: We analyzed data on the first 425 confirmed cases in Wuhan to determine the epidemiologic characteristics of NCIP.

primer.heading: What they did
primer.body: Field teams interviewed patients, relatives and health care workers. They recorded when each person fell ill, when they saw a doctor, and what they had been exposed to in the two weeks before. From a few well-documented cases and clusters they estimated two time gaps: the incubation period (infection to symptoms) and the serial interval (one case's symptoms to the next linked case's symptoms). They then fitted a transmission model to the early rise in cases that were not linked to the market. From this they worked out the growth rate, the doubling time and R0.

primer.heading: What they found
primer.body: More than half of the earliest cases were linked to the market. After the market closed, fewer than one in ten were. Symptoms began on average about 5 days after infection, and linked cases fell ill about 7.5 days apart. The epidemic doubled roughly every week. Combining that growth speed with the 7.5-day gap gives an R0 of about 2.2: each case was infecting about two others.
primer.quote: In its early stages, the epidemic doubled in size every 7.4 days. With a mean serial interval of 7.5 days (95% CI, 5.3 to 19), the basic reproductive number was estimated to be 2.2 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.9).

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: An R0 above 1 means the outbreak keeps growing unless transmission is cut by more than half. The incubation estimate supported a 14-day quarantine for exposed people. The estimates are early and rough, though. Testing was scarce at first, mild cases were probably missed, and some numbers rest on a handful of patients. That is why the ranges are wide, for example 1.4 to 3.9 for R0.
primer.quote: Our estimate was based on information from 10 cases and is somewhat imprecise; it would be important for further studies to provide more information on this distribution.

concepts.title: Clues that the virus was spreading person to person
concepts.idea: When the share of cases linked to the original source falls sharply while total cases keep rising, and cases cluster among close contacts, the infection must be passing between people.

terms.means: A patient who reported exposure to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market, the suspected original source
An infection caught directly from animals or their surroundings rather than from another person
A small group of linked cases among people in close contact, where one person's illness follows another's
The virus passing from one infected person to another

concepts.recap: Once the market link fades while cases keep climbing, and illness runs through close contacts and health care workers, the best explanation is that people are infecting people.

understand.explanation: At first, most patients had visited one seafood market, so each early market-linked case could have been a zoonotic infection, caught from animals or the market itself. Then the picture changed: 55% of patients who fell ill before January 1 had a market link, but only 8.6% of later patients did, and cases with no market link kept rising fast even after the market closed. The team also found more than one cluster of illness among close contacts, where one person fell ill and then another, and a growing share of cases among health care workers, who meet the virus through patients. No single clue settles it, and changes in case definitions and testing affect the numbers. Together, though, the clues point to human-to-human transmission among close contacts since mid-December 2019.
understand.quote: Although the majority of the earliest cases were linked to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market and the patients could have been infected through zoonotic or environmental exposures, it is now clear that human-to-human transmission has been occurring and that the epidemic has been gradually growing in recent weeks.

activities.question: A new illness appears in a city. Most of the first patients had visited one food market. A few weeks later, most new patients have never been near that market, and the number of patients keeps climbing even after the market is shut. What is your first guess about what is going on?

options.text: The virus is now spreading from person to person.
options.feedback: A strong first instinct. Keep it in mind: the evidence ahead tests whether the clues really support it, and which clues matter most.

options.text: The market is still the main source; the newer patients just forgot they went there.
options.feedback: Faulty memory is a fair worry, since exposure histories come from interviews. But could forgetting explain cases still rising after the market closed? Watch for that in the evidence.

options.text: Another animal source somewhere else in the city is infecting people.
options.feedback: That is possible in principle, and it is why a falling market share alone is not proof. Look out for clues that point specifically to people, not animals.

options.text: There is no way to tell yet.
options.feedback: Caution is healthy with early data. The stages ahead show how several separate clues can add up to a confident conclusion, even when each is imperfect.

activities.prompt: Reveal the evidence from the first 425 confirmed cases in Wuhan, one clue at a time. Ask yourself after each: does this point to animals, or to people?

stages.label: 1. The starting point
stages.text: On December 29, 2019, hospitals reported the first 4 cases of a pneumonia with no known cause. All 4 were linked to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market. A patient who reported exposure to this market is called a market-linked case. At this stage the patients could have caught it directly from animals or the market environment. That is a zoonotic infection: one caught from animals, not from another person.

stages.label: 2. The market share collapses
stages.text: The team split patients by when they fell ill. Among those with onset before January 1, 2020 (the day the market was closed), 55% were market-linked. Among later patients, only 8.6% were. The original source now explains only a small slice of new illness.

stages.label: 3. Yet cases keep rising
stages.text: If only the market were infecting people, closing it should make new cases dry up. Instead, the paper reports an exponential increase in cases with no market link, beginning in late December. Something other than the market was producing new patients.

stages.label: 4. Illness runs through close contacts
stages.text: The team investigated 5 clusters of cases. A cluster is a small group of linked patients in close contact, where one falls ill and then another does some days later. That pattern is what you expect when one person infects the next, which is called human-to-human transmission.

stages.label: 5. Health care workers fall ill
stages.text: The share of cases among health care workers gradually rose across three time periods. Their main exposure is the patients they treat, not a seafood market. The paper notes the share was still lower than in the earlier SARS and MERS outbreaks.

stages.label: 6. Reasons for care
stages.text: The numbers are not perfect measurements. Early on, the definition of a suspected case could rely on a market link, which may have drawn attention to market visitors. On January 18 the definition changed to travel to Wuhan or contact with patients from Wuhan. Testing kits reached Wuhan on January 11, and exposure histories came from interviews. Each of these can shift the shares, which is why no single clue is decisive on its own.

activities.takeaway: No single clue proves person-to-person spread. A shrinking market share, cases rising after the market closed, clusters among close contacts and infected health care workers all point the same way, and together they make the case.

activities.title: What does each clue point to?
activities.prompt: Sort each piece of information from the paper by what it mainly tells us.

groups.label: Points to the market or animal source
A reason for caution about the numbers

cards.text: 55% of patients who fell ill before January 1 were market-linked
cards.feedback: This fits an early outbreak driven largely by the market. On its own it says the source mattered early on, not that people were passing it on.

cards.text: Only 8.6% of patients who fell ill on or after January 1 were market-linked
cards.feedback: Most later patients had no market link, so something else was infecting them. Combined with the other clues, people are the likeliest source.

cards.text: Cases with no market link rose exponentially from late December
cards.feedback: Fast growth among patients who never visited the market is hard to explain by the market. It is what an infection passed from person to person would produce.

cards.text: The first 4 reported cases were all linked to the market
cards.feedback: This is why the market was the first suspect. It is about the start of the outbreak, not about how it spread later.

cards.text: The team investigated 5 clusters of cases among close contacts
cards.feedback: Linked illnesses among close contacts, falling ill one after another, are the most direct sign of one person infecting the next.

cards.text: The share of cases among health care workers rose over time
cards.feedback: Health care workers meet the virus through patients, so their infections point to spread from person to person.

cards.text: The early suspected-case definition could rely on a link to the market
cards.feedback: If doctors were looking for market visitors, early market-linked shares may be inflated. This affects how far we can trust the 55% versus 8.6% contrast on its own.

cards.text: Testing kits only reached Wuhan on January 11
cards.feedback: More testing finds more cases, so some of the rise in January reflects better detection, not only more infections. It is a limit on the numbers, not a clue about the source.

activities.takeaway: Several separate clues point to people, a couple describe the market's early role, and the caveats explain why the conclusion rests on all the clues together rather than any one figure.

activities.question: Look back at your first guess. Which set of evidence makes the strongest case that the virus was passing between people in Wuhan?

options.text: The fall in market-linked cases from 55% to 8.6%, on its own
options.feedback: This is an important clue, but on its own it could also reflect another animal source or a change in how cases were defined and found. It needs support from other clues.

options.text: The rise in the total number of cases, on its own
options.feedback: Total cases could rise if many people were still catching it from animals, or simply because testing improved. Rising totals alone do not say where infections came from.

options.text: A falling market share, non-linked cases rising after the market closed, clusters among close contacts and infected health care workers, taken together
options.feedback: Correct. Each clue has weaknesses, but they all point the same way. That agreement is why the paper concludes that human-to-human transmission had occurred among close contacts since mid-December 2019.

options.text: The fact that the first cases were linked to the market
options.feedback: This points the other way: it suggests the outbreak began with an animal or environmental source. It tells us where the outbreak started, not how it spread later.

hints: Which option combines more than one kind of evidence?
Think about which clues would be hard to explain if only the market were infecting people.

concepts.title: Growth rate and doubling time
concepts.idea: A steady daily growth rate r makes cases double every ln(2)/r days, so a rate of 0.10 per day means doubling about every week.

predict.question: Imagine control measures had cut Wuhan's early growth rate from 0.10 to 0.07 per day (a made-up scenario). Roughly how often would cases double then?
options: About every 5 days
About every 10 days
Still about every 7 days
About every 3 weeks
why: This gets the direction backwards. A lower rate means slower growth, so the doubling time gets longer, not shorter.
Right: 0.69 ÷ 0.07 ≈ 9.9, so about 10 days. Cutting the rate by 30% stretches the doubling time by about 40%, because the two are inversely related.
It is tempting to think a small change in rate barely matters. But the doubling time is ln 2 divided by the rate, so any change in r changes it.
Three weeks would need a rate near 0.03. Cutting the rate by under a third does not triple the doubling time. It stretches it by the inverse of the cut: 0.10 ÷ 0.07 ≈ 1.4 times.

terms.means: The fraction by which cases increase each day, written r. A rate of 0.10 per day is roughly 10% more cases each day.
Growth where cases rise by the same fraction every day, so they double over equal stretches of time.
The number of days it takes for case numbers to double.

model.title: Cases climbing day by day
model.note: Teaching model: cases rise smoothly at one fixed daily rate from a chosen starting count. It has no randomness, no reporting delays and no slowdown. Numbers are illustrative. The only figures from the paper are the ones cited in the text (0.10 per day, doubling in 7.4 days).

steps.say: This rising line counts cases, day by day, over six weeks.
This slider sets how fast cases grow each day. Watch the line steepen.
These lines mark when cases reach 2, 4 and 8 times where they started.
This slider sets how many cases you start with.
These boxes show the days to double, the daily rise and the cases on day 28.

explore.prompt: Now steer the curve yourself. Use the rule you just saw: days to double = 0.69 ÷ rate.

goals.text: Make cases double about once a week, as they did in early Wuhan.
hints: Which control changes how many days a doubling takes?
Right now cases double in about two weeks. A one-week doubling is half that time.
Doubling the rate halves the days to double.

goals.text: Reach at least 160 cases by day 28 while cases still take 7 days or more to double.
hints: Speeding up growth alone breaks the 7-day limit. Look at the other control too.
The starting-cases slider lifts the whole curve without changing the days to double.
Set the rate just under the one-week pace, then raise the start until the day-28 box clears 160.

feedback.correct: Yes. Doubling time is ln 2 (about 0.69) divided by the rate: 0.69 ÷ 0.07 ≈ 10 days. A slower rate gives a longer doubling time, in inverse proportion.
feedback.incorrect: The doubling time is not fixed, and it does not scale up with the rate. It equals 0.69 divided by the rate, so lowering r from 0.10 to 0.07 stretches it from about 7 to about 10 days.

steps.say: Start slow: r = 0.05 per day, about 5% more cases each day. This daily fraction is the growth rate.
Cases hit 2× at about day 14, 4× at day 28 and 8× near day 42. The gaps are equal: going from 10 to 20 takes as long as going from 40 to 80.
Rising by the same fraction every day is called exponential growth. The fixed time per doubling is the doubling time: here about 13.9 days.
Now make the rate four times bigger: 0.20 per day. The doubling time falls to about 3.5 days, a quarter as long.
That is the rule: doubling time = ln 2 ÷ r, about 0.69 ÷ r. Double the rate and you halve the doubling time.
Double the starting cases to 20. The curve sits higher, but the doubling lines don't move. Doubling time depends only on the rate.
Back to 10 cases. At 0.20 per day they become about 2,700 by day 28, roughly eight doublings. At 0.05 it was about 40. Small daily rates make huge gaps within weeks.

understand.explanation: When an epidemic grows by a steady fraction each day, each doubling takes the same number of days, however big the outbreak already is. That number, the doubling time, equals ln 2 (about 0.69) divided by the daily growth rate r. A rate of 0.10 per day, roughly 10% more cases each day, gives about 0.69 ÷ 0.10 ≈ 7 days. The paper fitted a transmission model to Wuhan cases with onset between December 10 and January 4 that were not linked to the market. It estimated r = 0.10 per day and a doubling time of 7.4 days; the small gap from 6.9 likely reflects rounding and how the uncertain estimates were summarised. Both numbers are uncertain: the doubling time's 95% interval runs from 4.2 to 14 days.
understand.quote: In the epidemic curve up to January 4, 2020, the epidemic growth rate was 0.10 per day (95% CI, 0.050 to 0.16) and the doubling time was 7.4 days (95% CI, 4.2 to 14).

connect.caption: This is the model's rule. The paper reports both r and the doubling time but does not print this formula; it is the standard link between them for steady exponential growth. r is the daily rate slider, n₀ is the starting-cases slider, and T_d is the 'Days to double' box.

concepts.recap: Doubling time = ln 2 ÷ growth rate: Wuhan's early rate of about 0.10 per day meant cases doubled roughly every week (the paper's estimate: 7.4 days).

concepts.title: Why the epidemic curve seemed to fall
concepts.idea: Because recent cases have not yet been diagnosed and reported, a still-growing epidemic looks as if it is declining at the end of the curve, so growth must be estimated from an earlier window.

predict.question: A health agency plots cases by the day each person fell ill. The last 10 days before its data cut-off are falling. Two weeks later it re-plots the same days, adding every case reported since. If the epidemic really kept growing, what will those 10 days look like now?
options: They fill in and now rise
They still fall, because counts for past days are final
They fall even more steeply
They level off into a flat plateau
why: Right. The missing cases were people already ill but not yet reported. As their reports arrive they are added to the days they fell ill, so the late days fill in and the rise reappears.
It is tempting to treat a past day's count as settled. But the curve is plotted by the day people fell ill, so later reports are added back to earlier days and those counts keep growing for weeks.
This would only happen if cases were removed over time. New reports only add cases to past days, so the late days can only go up.
A plateau would need new infections to stop rising. Here they kept growing, so once the delayed reports arrive the counts keep climbing rather than levelling off.

terms.means: A chart of cases plotted by the day each person fell ill
The time between someone falling ill and their case appearing in the data
Cases that exist but have not yet been found and counted

model.title: True cases versus cases counted by the cut-off
model.note: Teaching model: true cases grow at one fixed daily rate. Each case waits a random time before being counted, with an exponential spread around the average you set. The wait and the testing effort never change over time. Day 42 is the data cut-off. The vertical axis rescales to fit the true curve, so starting cases only change the scale. Numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data. The only paper figures cited are the 0.10-per-day growth rate and the measured delays from falling ill to hospital admission.

controls.label: Average wait before a case is counted (days)

outputs.label: Growth read from days 34–40 (per day)
outputs.expr: r + (ln(1 - exp(-2 / max(delay, 0.1))) - ln(1 - exp(-8 / max(delay, 0.1)))) / 6

outputs.label: Growth read from days 0–24 (per day)
outputs.expr: r + (ln(1 - exp(-18 / max(delay, 0.1))) - ln(1 - exp(-42 / max(delay, 0.1)))) / 24

outputs.label: Counted so far, of people ill a week before cut-off

series.label: Counted by the cut-off
series.expr: max(0, n0 * exp(r * x) * (1 - exp(-(42 - x) / max(delay, 0.1))))

steps.say: Same picture as before. The solid curve is true cases climbing at a steady daily rate, now plotted by the day each person fell ill.
New: the dashed curve shows only the cases that have been counted by the data cut-off on day 42.
This new slider sets how long a case waits, on average, before it is counted. It starts at zero, so the two curves match exactly.

explore.prompt: Now make the counting delay fool you. Tune the growth and the wait so the dashed curve tells a story the true curve doesn't.

goals.text: Make the counted data look like it's shrinking in its last days (negative growth read from days 34–40), while true cases double in 5 days or less.
hints: Two things must hold at once: fast true growth, and a falling tail in the dashed curve.
First speed up the true growth until 'True days to double' reads 5 or less. Then watch the late growth reading.
Faster growth fights the dip, so a short wait won't be enough. Raise the wait one day at a time until the late reading turns negative.

goals.text: Make the counted curve peak more than two weeks before the cut-off.
hints: Where the counted curve peaks depends on two things, not one.
Push the wait as long as it goes and check the peak day. Still not early enough? Try changing how fast true cases grow.
Slower true growth means a gentler rise near the end, so the missing recent cases win out earlier. Lower the daily rate step by step.

feedback.correct: Yes. Cases are filed under the day people fell ill, so late reports fill in the recent days. The apparent fall was a counting gap, not fewer infections.
feedback.incorrect: The dip came from cases not yet reported, not from fewer people falling ill. Each report is added to the day that person fell ill, so the late days fill in as reports arrive and the rise reappears.

steps.say: Set true growth to 0.10 per day, the paper's early estimate for Wuhan, and turn off the counting wait. The dashed curve sits right on the solid one.
This chart of cases by the day each person fell ill is called an epidemic curve. Now let each case take about 3 days on average to be counted. Only the last few days sag.

That wait is a reporting delay. Stretch it to 9 days, close to the average the paper found between falling ill and hospital admission in early January. Now the dashed curve peaks well before the cut-off.
Only about half of the people who fell ill a week before the cut-off are counted so far. Cases that exist but aren't yet found are called under-ascertainment.
Read growth from the last days and you get a negative number. The epidemic seems to be shrinking, yet the true rate is still 0.10 per day.
Read it from days 0 to 24 instead. Those cases have had weeks to be counted, so the estimate lands close to the true 0.10.

That's the lesson: true cases still soar, the counted curve falls, and only the earlier window tells the truth. If day 42 stands for January 22, this window roughly matches the paper's December 10 to January 4.

understand.explanation: An epidemic curve files each case under the day the person fell ill. But a case only appears once it has been found, tested and reported. People who fell ill shortly before the cut-off mostly haven't been counted yet. So the curve sags at its right edge even while true infections keep rising. The paper saw this drop in its Wuhan curve and judged it to be under-ascertainment, not a real turning point. It estimated growth only from cases that began by January 4, although its data ran to January 22. Its stated reason was that awareness and testing rose after the outbreak was announced, which changes the share of cases found. Caveat: this model uses one fixed delay. Real delays and testing changed over time, and that also bends the curve.
understand.quote: The development of the epidemic follows an exponential growth in cases, and a decline in the most recent days is likely to be due to under-ascertainment of cases with recent onset and delayed identification and reporting rather than a true turning point in incidence (Figure 1).

check.task: Show that a peak in the counted curve is not a turning point: make the counted curve peak more than a week before the cut-off while true cases still double in under 10 days.
check.hint: A long wait pulls the counted peak earlier. But true cases must still double within 10 days, so don't slow growth too much.
check.misconception: A peak followed by a drop in the reported curve means the epidemic has turned. In fact, a reporting delay alone can create that shape while infections keep climbing.

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule; the paper gives no equation for it. The first part is the true exponential curve, set by starting cases n₀ and the daily rate r. The bracket is the share of people who fell ill on day t who are counted by the day-42 cut-off, when the average wait is D. It shrinks towards zero as t nears the cut-off.

concepts.recap: A late dip in an epidemic curve can be nothing but uncounted recent cases. Read growth from an earlier window that has had time to fill in.

concepts.title: The serial interval: how far apart linked cases fall ill
concepts.idea: The serial interval is the spread of delays between one person's illness onset and the onset of the person they infected, and the paper estimated a mean of 7.5 days from only 6 pairs.

predict.question: Suppose a later team measured 60 linked pairs from the same outbreak, and the gaps turned out just as spread out as before. Compared with the 6-pair estimate, what should happen to the plausible range for the average gap?
options: It shrinks to about a third as wide
It stays about the same width
It shrinks to a tenth as wide
The individual gaps bunch up more tightly
why: Right: the range shrinks with the square root of the number of pairs. Ten times the pairs gives √10 ≈ 3.2, so the range is about a third as wide.
Tempting if you think the spread of gaps fixes the uncertainty. The spread stays the same, but averaging over more pairs pins the average down much better.
Tempting if uncertainty fell in step with the number of pairs. It falls with the square root, so ten times the pairs gives roughly a third, not a tenth.
This mixes up two things. More pairs make us surer of the average. They do not change how varied real gaps are, because that variation belongs to the disease.

terms.means: The number of days between one person's illness onset and the illness onset of someone they infected
The full pattern of how often each value turns up, not just a single typical value
A range of values for an estimate that fits the data; narrow means well pinned down, wide means very uncertain

model.title: Days between one person falling ill and the next person in the chain falling ill
model.note: Teaching model: the curve is a gamma curve set by its average and spread, the same kind of curve the paper fitted. The range for the average uses a simple textbook approximation (average ± 1.96 × spread ÷ √pairs), so it is symmetric and narrower than the paper's own 95% interval of 5.3 to 19 days. The paper's interval also drew on a prior based on SARS. The starting values of 7.5 and 3.4 days and 6 pairs are the paper's. Other settings are illustrative.

steps.say: This curve shows gaps in days. Each gap is how long after one person falls ill the person they infected falls ill. Higher on the curve means that gap is more common.
This slider moves the average gap. Watch the curve and its middle line slide right.
This one sets how spread out the gaps are, from tightly bunched to widely scattered.
This last slider is how many linked pairs were measured. The two outer lines show where the true average could plausibly sit, given that many pairs.

explore.prompt: Play with how much evidence you have and how varied the gaps are, and watch how well the average gets pinned down.

goals.text: Keep the gaps as spread out as the paper found, and make the range for the average narrower than 2 days.
hints: Which slider stands for how much evidence you collected?
In the walkthrough, four times the pairs only halved the range. You need it to shrink further than that.
The range shrinks with the square root of the number of pairs. Look somewhere between 40 and 60 pairs.

goals.text: Now suppose you are stuck with only 6 pairs, as the paper was. Get the range for the average below 3 days anyway.
hints: If you can't collect more pairs, what about the gaps themselves would make their average easier to pin down?
Try a disease whose gaps are more tightly bunched.
The spread has to come down to a bit under 2 days.

feedback.correct: Yes. The uncertainty in the average shrinks with the square root of the number of pairs. Ten times the pairs makes the range about a third as wide, while the real variety of gaps stays the same.
feedback.incorrect: The spread of individual gaps is a property of the disease and does not shrink with more data. What shrinks is the uncertainty in the average, and it falls with the square root of the number of pairs, so ten times the pairs gives about a third the width.

steps.say: Here are the paper's numbers. On average, 7.5 days passed between one person's illness onset and the onset of someone they infected. This delay is called the serial interval.
The gap is not the same for every pair. Some pairs fall ill a few days apart, and some more than two weeks apart. So the serial interval is a whole distribution, with a spread of about 3.4 days.

Now the catch. The paper had only 6 linked pairs, from 5 family or contact clusters. With so few, even the average is uncertain. In this simple model it could plausibly sit anywhere from about 5 to 10 days.
Suppose there were four times as many pairs. The range for the average halves. Uncertainty falls with the square root of the number of pairs, so it falls slowly.
Back to 6 pairs, but now imagine the gaps were tightly bunched. Then even a few pairs would tell you the average fairly well. A wide spread makes a small sample much less informative.

Back at the paper's real case. Its own range, a 95% confidence interval, ran from 5.3 to 19 days. It is wider and lopsided because it used a fitted curve and a SARS-based starting guess. So 7.5 days is a best guess, not a settled fact.

understand.explanation: When one person infects another, you usually can't see the moment of infection, but you can see when each falls ill. The serial interval is the gap between those two illness onsets, and it varies from pair to pair, so it is described as a distribution with an average and a spread. The team traced 5 clusters of cases, found 6 infector–infected pairs, and fitted a gamma curve to their onset gaps: an average of 7.5 days, give or take 3.4. Because only 6 pairs were available, the average is very uncertain: the paper's 95% confidence interval runs from 5.3 to 19 days. More pairs, or less varied gaps, would narrow that range.
understand.quote: On the basis of the dates of illness onset of 6 pairs of cases in these clusters, we estimated that the serial interval distribution had a mean (±SD) of 7.5±3.4 days (95% CI, 5.3 to 19) (Figure 2B).

connect.caption: This is the model's simple rule, not an equation from the paper. μ is the average gap (7.5 days in the paper), σ is the spread of gaps (3.4 days), and n is the number of linked pairs (6). The paper fitted a gamma curve with a SARS-based prior, which gave a wider, lopsided 95% CI of 5.3 to 19 days.

concepts.recap: The serial interval is the gap between linked cases' illness onsets. The paper's average of 7.5 days rests on just 6 pairs, so it is a rough estimate with a wide range.

activities.title: Reading gaps off a made-up chain of cases

steps.text: Imagine a chain: A infects B, and B infects C. Investigators can't see when anyone was infected, but they do know when each person fell ill.
A falls ill on day 0. B falls ill on day 8. C falls ill on day 15.
Gap for the pair A → B: 8 − 0.
Gap for the pair B → C: 15 − 8.
Two pairs give two different gaps. Their average is (8 + 7) ÷ 2.
Two pairs can't tell you much. Another chain might show gaps of 3 and 14 days. The paper had only 6 such pairs.

activities.takeaway: Each infector–infected pair gives one gap between illness onsets. Gaps differ from pair to pair, so you need many pairs to know their average well. These numbers are made up, and matching the paper's 7.5 is a coincidence.

concepts.title: R0 and the line between growth and fade-out
concepts.idea: If each case infects R others per generation, case numbers multiply by R each generation, so the outbreak grows when R is above 1 and dies out when it is below 1.

predict.question: A cut of about 55% in transmission stops growth if R₀ is 2.2. But the paper's 95% interval for R₀ ran from 1.4 to 3.9. If the true R₀ were at the top of that range, would the same 55% cut still stop growth?
options: Yes: a cut that works for 2.2 works across the whole range
No: at 3.9 each case would still infect about 1.8 others, so cases would keep growing
No: no cut can ever stop an outbreak whose R₀ is above 2
It would hold cases exactly flat
why: Tempting, because 2.2 is the headline estimate. But the cut only removes a share of transmission: 3.9 × 0.45 ≈ 1.8, which is still above 1.

Right. What matters is the number left after the cut: 3.9 × 0.45 ≈ 1.75. That is above 1, so each round is bigger than the last. The uncertainty in R₀ carries straight into how much control is needed.
A bigger R₀ needs a bigger cut, but some cut always works. At 3.9, removing roughly three of every four infections brings the number below 1.
Flat would need exactly 1 infection per case after the cut. At the top of the range the number is about 1.75, well above the line, so cases grow.

terms.means: The average number of people one case infects when nobody in the population is immune yet and nothing is done to stop it
The average number of people one case actually infects once control measures are in place; the aim of control is to push it below 1

model.title: Cases, round by round of infection
model.note: Teaching model: every case infects exactly the same average number of people, and each round of infection is one serial interval. Rounds are really separate steps but are drawn as a smooth curve. Nobody becomes immune, and the outbreak starts from 10 cases. The paper itself fitted a renewal-equation transmission model to Wuhan onset dates. The figure of about 2.2 infections per case is the paper's estimate and the figure of about 3 for SARS is quoted in the paper; all other numbers are illustrative.

controls.label: New infections per case, with no control

outputs.label: New infections per case, after the cut

x.label: Round of infection (each round ≈ one serial interval)

steps.say: Every round, each sick person passes the virus on to some new people. This curve counts the new cases in each round, starting from 10.
This slider sets how many people one case infects when nobody does anything to stop it.
This one is control measures, such as isolation and quarantine. They cut transmission by a percentage. Watch the solid curve bend down.
The dashed curve is the outbreak with no control. The flat line marks each case only replacing itself.
These boxes count the cases five and eight rounds in.

explore.prompt: Now use control measures yourself. Find the cut that just tips the outbreak from growing to fading, and no bigger. Cutting more than needed costs a city a lot.

goals.text: Keep the no-control number at the paper's estimate of 2.2. Find the smallest cut that stops cases from growing.
hints: Growth stops when each case, after the cut, infects fewer than one person.
Watch the 'after the cut' box as you raise the cut. Stop at the first setting where it drops below 1.
Halving transmission isn't quite enough. You need a little more than half.

goals.text: SARS spread at about 3 infections per case and was brought under control. Find the smallest cut that would stop an outbreak like that from growing.
hints: First make the no-control number match SARS.
Then raise the cut until the after-cut number falls below 1, and go no further.
With 3 infections per case, you must remove a bit more than two of every three infections.

feedback.correct: Yes. A fixed cut only removes a share of transmission. If the true R₀ is higher, the same share leaves more than one infection per case, and the outbreak keeps growing. So the paper's wide uncertainty interval matters for planning.
feedback.incorrect: The cut multiplies R₀; it does not set the result directly. At the top of the paper's range, 3.9 × 0.45 ≈ 1.75, which is still above 1. Growth stops only when the number left after the cut is below 1.

steps.say: Say each case infects 2 people. Ten cases make 20, then 40, then 80. The count multiplies by 2 every round, so by round 5 there are 320.
Now each case infects exactly 1 person. Ten cases stay ten. Each case only replaces itself, so the curve sits on the flat line.
Just below 1: 10, then 8, then 6.4. The outbreak fades even though every case still infects someone. By round 8 fewer than 2 cases are left.

Just above 1, it slowly but surely grows: 10 becomes about 43 by round 8. This average number of people infected by one case, in a population where nobody is immune, is the basic reproductive number (R₀). The value 1 is the knife-edge.
The paper estimated R₀ ≈ 2.2 for Wuhan's early epidemic. Ten cases become about 500 by round 5, and the curve shoots off the chart.
Control measures don't have to stop every infection. They lower the reproductive number, which is the number each case actually infects. A 30% cut leaves about 1.54: still growing.
Halve transmission and each case still infects 1.1 people. Growth is far slower than the dashed curve, but it is still growth. Halving is not quite enough.

understand.explanation: If each case infects R people on average, every round of infection multiplies the case count by R. Above 1, the count multiplies up round after round. Below 1, it shrinks toward zero. At exactly 1, it holds steady. The paper estimated the basic reproductive number (R₀) at about 2.2 (95% CI 1.4 to 3.9), from the growth of Wuhan cases up to January 4 combined with the serial interval. Even the low end of that range is above 1, which means the outbreak would keep growing without control. Control measures aim to push the reproductive number below 1. The paper notes that SARS, with an R₀ near 3, was controlled by isolation and infection control. R₀ is an average, though: real cases vary, super-spreading can occur, and this estimate came from early, incomplete data.
understand.quote: We estimated an R0 of approximately 2.2, meaning that on average each patient has been spreading infection to 2.2 other people. In general, an epidemic will increase as long as R0 is greater than 1, and control measures aim to reduce the reproductive number to less than 1.

connect.caption: This is the teaching model's rule, not the paper's renewal-equation model. R₀ is the first slider. It is multiplied by the share of transmission left after the cut, which the second slider sets. Together they give the number each case actually infects (the 'after the cut' box). That number is raised to the power of the round number g. If it is above 1, the power explodes; if it is below 1, it shrinks toward zero.

concepts.recap: Cases multiply by R each round of infection, so the epidemic grows above R = 1 and fades below it; control must push R under 1.

concepts.title: Turning doubling time into R0
concepts.idea: R0 is the growth rate seen across one serial interval, so the same doubling time implies a larger R0 when the serial interval is longer.

predict.question: Two new outbreaks both have cases doubling every 7 days. In city A, linked patients fall ill about 4 days apart. In city B, they fall ill about 10 days apart. In which city is each case infecting more people?
options: City A, with the 4-day gap
City B, with the 10-day gap
The same in both, because they double equally fast
You can't say without watching infections happen
why: A short gap can feel like 'faster spread', but the growth speed is already fixed. With a short gap, each case only has to infect a few people for cases to double every 7 days.
Right. In 10 days, cases doubling every 7 days grow by well over twice. Each generation must be much bigger than the last, so each case is infecting more people.
It is tempting to read R0 straight from the doubling time. But R0 is growth per generation, and the generations are a different length in each city.
This is the point of the method. The doubling speed and the gap between linked illnesses together let you work out R0 without observing any single infection.

terms.means: A rule that builds today's new cases from earlier cases, weighted by how many days ago those earlier cases fell ill

model.title: How many people each case infects, from growth speed and the gap between linked illnesses
model.note: Teaching model: it uses the standard result for a steadily growing outbreak whose gaps between linked illnesses follow a gamma distribution, the shape the paper fitted. The spread of the gaps is fixed at the paper's SD of 3.4 days, and only the average gap moves. With the paper's central values (growth 0.10 per day, 7.5-day gap), this formula gives about 2.0. The paper's 2.2 came from its full fitted model, which averaged over uncertainty and used a SARS-based prior for the gap. Other slider positions are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: Average days between linked patients falling ill

steps.say: This solid curve answers one question: for a given speed of growth, how many people must each case be infecting?
This slider sets how fast cases grow each day. Watch the marker and the dot slide along the curve.
This slider sets the average number of days between one patient falling ill and the person they infected falling ill. Watch the solid curve bend.
The dashed curve keeps Wuhan's 7.5-day gap fixed for comparison. The flat line at 1 marks where an outbreak only just holds steady.

explore.prompt: Use the two sliders to build outbreaks of your own. Remember that how many people each case infects depends on both the growth speed and the gap.

goals.text: Make an outbreak where cases double in about a week, yet each case infects only about 1.5 people.
hints: First get the doubling time near a week. Then ask what makes each generation smaller.
With the growth fixed, a shorter gap fits less growth into each generation.
Keep the growth near Wuhan's and bring the gap well below Wuhan's 7.5 days.

goals.text: Give the virus a gap about twice as long as Wuhan's, then find the growth speed at which each case still infects about 2.2 people.
hints: With a longer gap, the same growth speed would give a much bigger number. So which way must growth move?
Slow the growth rate down until the dot sits near the 2.2 line.
You'll need cases doubling much more slowly than once a week, somewhere around once every two weeks.

feedback.correct: Yes. R0 is the growth over one gap between linked illnesses. With the same doubling speed, a longer gap holds more growth, so each case must be infecting more people.
feedback.incorrect: You may have assumed the doubling speed alone settles R0. It doesn't: R0 is growth per generation. When generations are 10 days apart instead of 4, each one must be bigger to give the same 7-day doubling.

steps.say: Put in Wuhan's two measured ingredients. Cases grew about 0.10 per day (the paper's rounded figure; its 7.4-day doubling matches about 0.094). Linked patients fell ill 7.5 days apart on average.
Now count how much growth fits inside one gap. In 7.5 days, cases growing this fast double about once.
One gap is one generation: infector, then infected. If cases roughly double per generation, each case must be passing the virus on to about two people. The model reads about 2.0.
Keep the growth exactly the same, but suppose linked patients fell ill 12 days apart. More growth now fits inside each generation, so each case must infect about 3 people.

The paper's uncertainty range for the gap stretched to 19 days. With that gap, the same growth would imply over 6. This is why the uncertain gap matters so much, and why the paper also drew on SARS's known gap to steady its estimate.

The paper combined the two ingredients with a renewal equation. That rule builds each day's new cases from earlier cases, weighted by how long ago they fell ill. The curve here is what that rule gives for a steadily growing outbreak.

Just by timing how fast cases doubled and how many days apart linked patients fell ill, you can work out that each case infected about two others, without watching a single infection happen. The paper's full model said 2.2.

understand.explanation: The doubling time tells you how fast cases grow per day. The gap between linked illnesses tells you how many days one generation of infection takes. Put the two together and you get the growth over one generation. That is R0: how many new cases each case produces. So the same doubling time means a bigger R0 if the gap is longer, and a smaller R0 if it is shorter. The paper measured growth from cases with onset up to January 4, estimated the gap from only 6 pairs of linked cases, and fitted a renewal-equation model to get an R0 of 2.2. Its uncertainty range (1.4 to 3.9) is wide partly because the gap was so uncertain.
understand.quote: In the epidemic curve up to January 4, 2020, the epidemic growth rate was 0.10 per day (95% CI, 0.050 to 0.16) and the doubling time was 7.4 days (95% CI, 4.2 to 14). Using the serial interval distribution above, we estimated that R0 was 2.2 (95% CI, 1.4 to 3.9).

check.task: Keep cases growing exactly as fast as in Wuhan (0.10 per day), but put the model in a state where each case must be infecting more than 3 people.
check.hint: If the growth rate can't move, which other ingredient feeds into R0?
check.misconception: That the doubling time alone fixes R0, so two outbreaks that double equally fast must spread equally per case. R0 also depends on how long each generation of infection takes.

connect.caption: This is the model's rule, not an equation printed in the paper. It is the standard renewal-equation result for an outbreak growing at rate r (the growth slider) whose gaps between linked illnesses follow a gamma distribution with mean T (the gap slider) and SD σ, fixed here at the paper's 3.4 days. R0 is the output read off the curve. With σ near zero, the rule becomes simply e^{r×T}, the growth over one exact gap.

concepts.recap: R0 is growth measured across one generation of infection, so Wuhan's doubling time and 7.5-day serial interval together imply each case infected about two others.

The learner compares R = 2.2 (the paper's estimate) with R = 3 (the paper's figure for SARS) and R = 0.8. They see why control aims to push R below 1.
